Knowledge-base entry for 'Bacterial_Blight':
────────────────────────────────────────
Bacterial Blight (Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. glycinea) typically begins with small, angular, reddish-brown lesions that are surrounded by a yellow halo. These lesions are most commonly found in the upper canopy because young leaves are the most susceptible to infection. As the disease progresses, the lesions can grow together to form large, irregularly shaped dead areas. Centers of older lesions often fall out, giving leaves a tattered appearance. The disease is favored by cool temperatures and can be more prevalent after rainstorms with high winds. Bacterial Blight is often confused with other diseases, but its specific symptom of leaf tattering distinguishes it from some similar diseases, like Septoria brown spot.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Bacterial_Pustule':
────────────────────────────────────────
Bacterial Pustule (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines) symptoms typically appear mid to late season on the upper leaves of the plant. Initial lesions start as small, pale green specks with elevated centers, developing into larger, irregularly shaped infected areas. Each lesion is surrounded by a greenish-yellow halo. A pustule may form in the center of some lesions, usually visible on the lower leaf surface. Notably, bacterial pustule does not cause leaves to tatter as seen in bacterial blight. The disease thrives in hot, wet weather, and certain soybean varieties may be particularly susceptible, while others are marketed as resistant. In comparison to Bacterial Blight, which causes tattered leaves and has angular, reddish-brown lesions with yellow halos, bacterial pustule is characterized by its distinct pale green specks and the absence of leaf tattering.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Cercospora':
────────────────────────────────────────
Cercospora Leaf Blight (Cercospora kikuchii) symptoms usually appear on leaves in the uppermost canopy during the beginning of seed set. Initial symptoms include light purple, pinpoint spots that can expand into larger, irregularly shaped patches. Affected leaves may become leathery and exhibit dark purple with bronze highlights. In severe cases, symptoms can lead to defoliation, with petioles remaining attached to the plant. The disease develops in warm and wet conditions, favoring infection and symptom progression. Additionally, because of its visual characteristics, Cercospora leaf blight may be confused with sunburn, which typically appears on the underside of the leaf. A key difference from Sudden Death Syndrome is that Cercospora symptoms are often localized to upper canopy leaves and do not involve the rotting of taproots characteristic of SDS.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Bean_Pod_Mottle_virus':
────────────────────────────────────────
Bean Pod Mottle virus causes distinct mottling on soybean leaves, characterized by irregular, mosaic-like patterns of light green to yellowish discoloration, which can appear as raised spots or patches. These mottled areas may become necrotic, leading to dark, sunken lesions, especially along the leaf margins. Affected pods show similar yellow mottling and may develop a shriveled appearance, with seeds inside becoming discolored but typically without external gummosis or exudate present. The texture of the affected tissues is often rough or blistered, and the patterns can be distributed unevenly across the plant, with older leaves displaying more pronounced symptoms. The presence of soft, irregular halos surrounding lesions is notable, along with a potential reduction in pod size due to the overall stress on the plant. In contrast to Soybean Mosaic Virus, which primarily exhibits uniform leaf discoloration without the mottling patterns, Bean Pod Mottle virus uniquely combines light and dark coloration with a patchy distribution, making it distinct in visual identification.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Brown_Stem_Rot':
────────────────────────────────────────
The visual symptoms of Brown Stem Rot (Cadophora gregata) include chlorosis and necrosis between leaf veins, accompanied by leaf curling and leaf death. Symptoms can vary depending on the soybean variety and environmental conditions, and in some instances, no foliar symptoms may occur. Foliar symptoms typically appear after early pod set; however, stem symptoms usually occur before foliar symptoms and can manifest even when leaf symptoms are absent. Externally, infected stems may look healthy, but upon splitting, internal browning of vascular tissue and pith becomes evident, particularly at the nodes and in the lower stem. This internal discoloration can be a critical aspect for diagnosis. The key difference between Brown Stem Rot and Sudden Death Syndrome is that while both can produce similar foliar symptoms, the internal stem browning is a distinguishing feature of Brown Stem Rot, which will not be present in Sudden Death Syndrome.
────────────────────────────────────────
